rich_summary: This section recounts how King Dushmanta responds after hearing Sakuntala explain her origin as the adopted daughter of the sage Kanwa, who found her abandoned and protected by birds in the wilderness. Struck by her beauty and dignity, Dushmanta asks her to marry him according to the Gandharva form of marriage—a union based on mutual consent without formal rites. Sakuntala hesitates, wishing her father to give her away, but the king argues from religious law that such a marriage is acceptable for Kshatriyas. She agrees on one condition: the son born of their union must become the heir to his throne. Dushmanta promises and weds her before leaving for his capital. When Kanwa returns, he already knows what happened through spiritual insight and blesses the union, prophesying that their son will become a mighty ruler whose power will extend over the earth.

highlight_spans.why: Explains the origin of Sakuntala’s name and identity as a child protected by birds.
Dushmanta’s direct proposal captures the emotional turning point of the encounter.
The discussion of the eight forms of marriage provides key cultural and legal context from ancient Hindu law.
Sakuntala’s condition that her future son become heir establishes the political stakes of the union.
Kanwa’s prophetic blessing foreshadows the birth of a powerful ruler destined for greatness.

top_scenes.scene_text: King Dushmanta in the forest hermitage earnestly proposing marriage to Sakuntala amid trees and ascetic huts.
Sage Kanwa returning to the hermitage and calmly blessing the shy Sakuntala after divining her secret union.
A visionary moment of prophecy as Kanwa foretells that Sakuntala’s future son will rule mightily over the earth.
